pedagogy.summary: At 5-6, attending to precision means using mathematical words carefully — 'more than / fewer than / the same as' for comparing, shape names with 'sides' and 'corners', and positional words (above, below, next to) — and beginning to refine vague everyday language into words that pin down the meaning. The EEF Early Years guidance frames this as a staged informal→formal journey: start from a child's own words ('pointy', 'big') and help them rephrase precisely ('has points', 'taller'). A key move is exposing children to a WIDE VARIETY of examples of each shape so they do not form a narrow, prototype-bound concept (only a 'point-up' triangle counts).
bestPractices: Seize everyday moments to reinforce precise vocabulary — who is 'first', who has 'more than', where the teddy is 'behind' — rather than teaching words in isolation (EEF)
Help children refine ambiguous everyday words: when a child says 'big', ask 'taller, or more?' so they choose the word that carries the meaning (EEF's big→tall example)
Move informal→formal: accept 'pointy'/'curved' first, then introduce formal shape names gradually and reinforce them in routine (EEF)
Expose children to varied examples and non-examples of each shape (many kinds of triangle, tilted squares) to prevent an over-generalised, prototype-only concept (EEF)
Pair each word with the action or feature it names — run a finger along a SIDE, point to a CORNER — so the vocabulary is grounded, not recited
keyRepresentations: Comparison language with matched groups (more than / fewer than / same as)
A varied shape gallery (many triangles, rotated squares) with sides and corners traced
Real objects and manipulatives named in play
commonMisconceptions: Uses ambiguous everyday words where a precise one exists — 'big' for tall or for 'more', 'by' for a specific position (EEF)
Recognises only prototype shapes — rejects a long or upside-down triangle as 'not a triangle', calls a tilted square a 'diamond' (EEF: needs varied exposure)
Uses 'sides' and 'corners' interchangeably, or counts corners when asked for sides
Thinks a shape's name depends on how it is turned or how big it is, rather than its properties

learn.summary: For children aged 5-6, attending to precision means using mathematical words carefully: comparison words ('more than / fewer than / the same as'), shape vocabulary ('sides', 'corners', shape names), and positional words (above, below, behind, next to). A key proposed teaching move is to make vague language have a visible consequence so the child can discover the value of a precise word — a research-informed approach rather than a uniquely required method — following an informal→formal journey that starts from the child's own words ('pointy', 'big') and helps them rephrase ('has points', 'taller'). Children also need exposure to a WIDE VARIETY of examples of each shape so they do not form a narrow, prototype-bound concept.

activities.title: Tell the literal robot where teddy goes
feedback: When the child says 'by the box' and the robot puts teddy near the box but not where the child meant (e.g. behind it instead of on top), the mismatch itself is the feedback — prompt: 'Did the robot put teddy where you wanted? How could you say it so teddy lands exactly there?'
If the child says 'bigger' and is handed the taller-but-fewer tower, ask 'Do you mean taller, or more blocks?' and have the CHILD choose the precise word rather than supplying it.
When the child uses a precise word and the robot succeeds first time, name the success: 'On top of told the robot exactly where — it worked straight away.'
activities.rationale: Precision of communication becomes meaningful when vagueness has an immediate, repeatable consequence the child can see and repair. A responsive surface (or in-role character) lets the child produce and refine language rather than merely recognise it, following EEF's informal→formal refinement (big→tall). This is a proposed design, not a validated or uniquely-best format.
sourceClaims: Practitioners should reinforce precise vocabulary (first, more than, fewer) and help children refine ambiguous everyday words (e.g. 'big' → 'tall'); move from informal to formal language; and expose children to a wide variety of shapes (not just prototypes like equilateral triangles) to prevent a narrow shape concept
Mathematically proficient students communicate precisely, use clear definitions, and in the elementary grades give carefully formulated explanations to each other
learnerActions: Direct a friendly robot (or puppet/character) to place teddy somewhere, e.g. say 'put teddy by the box'.

Watch the robot do EXACTLY what the words say — 'by the box' only means near the box, so the robot might put teddy behind it, in front of it, or beside it — so the ambiguity can produce a result that is not where the child meant.
Refine the instruction to a precise positional word ('on top of the box', 'behind the box') and check the robot now gets it right.
Repeat with a comparison round: ask for 'the tower with MORE blocks' rather than 'the bigger tower', to distinguish taller from more.
Say, in the child's own words, why the exact word helped the robot understand.
activities.intendedInsight: A vague everyday word (like 'by' or 'big') often fails to pin down the meaning; choosing a precise word (on top of / behind; taller / more) lets a listener do exactly what you intend.

activities.title: A character who takes your words literally
feedback: When the character deliberately misunderstands, prompt the child to explain which precise word they meant.
Praise the moment the child spontaneously refines: 'You changed by to behind so I knew exactly where.'
activities.rationale: An in-role character who misunderstands can generate precise-language repair through unscripted, responsive dialogue, giving the child spoken production practice. Short turns suit the age. This is a proposed format; the sources do not establish it as superior to other media.
sourceClaims: Practitioners should reinforce precise vocabulary (first, more than, fewer) and help children refine ambiguous everyday words (e.g. 'big' → 'tall'); move from informal to formal language; and expose children to a wide variety of shapes (not just prototypes like equilateral triangles) to prevent a narrow shape concept
learnerActions: Talk with a playful character (puppet or robot friend) who cheerfully misunderstands vague instructions, e.g. 'You said BY the box, so I put teddy BEHIND it — right?'
Answer the character's clarifying questions to pin down the position, comparison, or shape word you meant.
Keep each exchange short, and restate the instruction precisely until the character gets it right.
activities.intendedInsight: Being asked 'did you mean this or that?' makes a child notice an ambiguity and reach for the word that removes it — the repair IS the practice.

activities.title: The varied shape gallery (sides, corners and non-prototypes)
feedback: If the child rejects a long or upside-down triangle, show more varied examples and non-examples and return focus to the defining property: a closed shape with three straight sides.
If the child calls a tilted square a 'diamond', count the four equal sides and four square (right-angle) corners together and confirm it is still a square however it is turned.
If the child swaps 'sides' and 'corners', re-pair each word with its action (run a finger along a side, point to a corner) in play rather than marking it wrong — it resolves with exposure.
activities.rationale: Varied examples and non-examples counter the prototype-only concept. A tap-to-reveal gallery can label and prime the vocabulary; on its own it primes recognition and does not require the child to produce or refine language, so pair it with the directing/dialogue activities.
sourceClaims: Practitioners should reinforce precise vocabulary (first, more than, fewer) and help children refine ambiguous everyday words (e.g. 'big' → 'tall'); move from informal to formal language; and expose children to a wide variety of shapes (not just prototypes like equilateral triangles) to prevent a narrow shape concept
learnerActions: Explore a gallery of many triangles and quadrilaterals shown in varied orientations and sizes — long thin triangles, upside-down triangles, tilted squares.
Trace a finger along each SIDE and point to each CORNER as they are named, then reveal the shape's name.

Decide whether a tilted square is still a square (it has four equal sides and four square corners, however it is turned) and whether a long or upside-down triangle is still a triangle (it is a closed shape with three straight sides).
Sort a tilted square into the 'square' group by its properties rather than by how it looks or how it is turned.
activities.intendedInsight: A shape's name depends on its properties (its straight sides and its corners), not on its size or orientation; 'side' and 'corner' name different features.

activities.title: Place the object in a spatial scene
feedback: If the placement does not match the word used, ask which word would describe where teddy actually is.
Confirm when the chosen word and the placement agree: 'Behind — and that's just where you put it.'
activities.rationale: Positional vocabulary is genuinely spatial, so placing an object in a scene (a simple room or picture) exercises that strand concretely. This supports only the positional strand; the comparison and shape-name strands are not spatial, so this activity is a companion rather than the main vehicle.
sourceClaims: Practitioners should reinforce precise vocabulary (first, more than, fewer) and help children refine ambiguous everyday words (e.g. 'big' → 'tall'); move from informal to formal language; and expose children to a wide variety of shapes (not just prototypes like equilateral triangles) to prevent a narrow shape concept
learnerActions: Place teddy in a scene above, below, behind, or next to another object, choosing the positional word that matches where you want it.
Describe aloud where you put teddy using the precise positional word.
Swap roles: a partner states a position and you place teddy to match, then check it agrees.
activities.intendedInsight: Positional language describes genuine spatial relationships; the right word lets another person find the object exactly.

constraints: Seize everyday moments to reinforce precise vocabulary — who is 'first', who has 'more than', where the teddy is 'behind' — rather than teaching words in isolation.

Build informal→formal: accept the child's own words ('pointy', 'curved', 'big') first, then introduce and reinforce formal words gradually; have the CHILD choose the precise word rather than simply supplying it.
Pair each word with the action or feature it names (run a finger along a side, point to a corner) so vocabulary is grounded, not recited.
Treat interchangeable use of 'sides' and 'corners' as a developmental stage that resolves with exposure, not an error to drill or mark wrong.

A picture-word matching or tap-to-reveal task can check or prime recognition but does not by itself elicit the child producing or refining language; use it as a warm-up alongside the directing/dialogue activities, not as the sole vehicle.
The spatial-scene activity supports only the positional strand; it does not exercise comparison or shape-name vocabulary.

Diagnostic prompts deliberately use an ambiguous word (e.g. 'by') so the vagueness is detectable; a precise word like 'behind' would not reveal whether the child attends to precision. Responses are surfaced for discussion, not marked right or wrong.

When naming a square, use the properties that define it (four equal sides and four square corners), so a non-square rhombus is not accepted as a square; the teaching point is that turning a shape does not change its identity.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were NOT re-fetched. The activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions, and citations support general teaching principles rather than proving any specific activity was tested.

The legacy entry asserted that precision 'is best taught' by a live surface with a literal robot and framed alternatives as unable to make the child produce or refine language. These comparative-necessity claims are not established by the sources; they have been softened to scoped proposals noting each format's affordance and limit, including in the summary.

Both cited sources (CCSS MP6 and EEF Early Maths) are general-practice guidance, not evaluations of the proposed robot game, puppet dialogue, or gallery; no comparative efficacy among these formats is established.

The original row defined a tilted square as a square by 'four equal sides' alone; this under-specifies a square (a rhombus also has four equal sides). Corrected in the learner action, feedback and constraints to include four square corners while keeping the age-appropriate focus on orientation invariance.

probeDeeper: If I said 'the cup is by the sink', show me two different places the cup could be.
Is this one [a long thin triangle] a triangle? How do you know?
Point to a side, and now a corner — which is which?
Sam says his tower is 'big'. What could you ask him so you know exactly what he means?
assess.correctAnswer: No single scored answer — listen for the child noticing that 'by' is vague (teddy could be on top, behind, beside, inside) and reaching for a precise positional word, and ideally saying why it matters (so the listener isn't confused). This is surfaced for discussion, not marked right or wrong.

errorPatterns.pattern: Uses an ambiguous everyday word where a precise one exists — 'big' for tall or for 'more', 'by' for a definite position — and does not notice the ambiguity
errorPatterns.nextMove: Model refining in the moment ('do you mean taller, or more blocks?') and have the CHILD choose the precise word; build informal→formal, don't just supply the answer.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Repeats 'by'/'big' contentedly and cannot say what else it might mean when shown alternatives

errorPatterns.pattern: Recognises only prototype shapes — rejects a long or upside-down triangle as 'not a triangle', or calls a tilted square a 'diamond'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Show a wide variety of examples and non-examples and focus on defining properties (three straight sides) rather than the look or orientation.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: On the triangle counterexample the child denies it is a triangle, or renames a rotated square

errorPatterns.pattern: Uses 'sides' and 'corners' interchangeably while the vocabulary is still forming
errorPatterns.nextMove: Do NOT drill definitions or treat it as an error to mark wrong; keep pairing each word with the action (trace a side, point to a corner) in play — it resolves with exposure.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Counts corners when asked for sides, or swaps the words, but self-corrects with modelling

responseLevels.gap: Uses vague everyday words and does not notice the ambiguity; names only prototype shapes; conflates sides and corners.
responseLevels.full: Unprompted, chooses precise comparison, shape and positional words, notices when a word is ambiguous and refines it, recognises varied (non-prototype) examples by their properties, and can say why saying it exactly helps the listener.
responseLevels.partial: When prompted, offers a more precise word (taller, on top of) and names common shapes, but does not spontaneously refine vague language or accept non-prototype examples.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: I'm going to tell you where teddy is: 'teddy is by the box.' Does that tell you EXACTLY where to find teddy, or could teddy be in lots of different places? Show me. How would you say it so I know exactly where teddy is?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who uses words loosely just repeats 'by' and is satisfied; a child attending to precision notices the ambiguity and refines it, showing awareness that a word must pin down the meaning. The prompt deliberately uses an ambiguous everyday word so the vagueness is detectable — a precise word like 'behind' would not separate the children.
